text.p: Campbell Soup Co's annointment of a successor to chief executive David Johnson and the one-year extension of Johnson's term as chairman will ensure a smooth transition to a new leader, analysts said.
Nevertheless, they said Dale Morrison, named Monday to succeed Johnson as president and chief executive officer from July 15, faces a huge challenge filling the shoes of the dynamic Johnson.

Johnson will remain as chairman until July 31, 1998, a year beyond the expiration of his current contract, Campbell said in its announcement Monday. A company spokesman said the board would name a new chairman closer to Johnson's departure.

Analysts said a 15/16 decline in Campbell's share price by early afternoon Monday to 48 7/16 reflected at least in part disappointment over the reduced role and eventual departure of Johnson. But they also said they expected a rebound, possibly aided by a Campbell share buyback.
"This is a good, solid manageable move, and I think that it's a process, not a one-off tranaction," Merrill Lynch analyst Leonard Teitelbaum said.
Referring to the possibility of a share buyback, he said, "They may well step in here."

Campbell's announcement ends months of speculation on the future of Johnson, a hard-driving Australian known for unchecked enthusiasm while rallying company employees and shareholders and for sharply reviving the earnings of a one-moribund company.

Although Johnson unveiled an ambitious restructuring plan last year aimed at aggressively boosting sales and earnings growth, he had kept close to the vest his own plans following the expiration of his five-year term as chairman.
"I think Campbell shareholders are a little disappointed that David Johnson is leaving so shortly into the new business plan," Prudential Securities analyst John McMillin said.
Said Janney Montgomery Scott analyst Mitchell Pinheiro, "I don't care how dynamic you are, you are going to pale in comparison to David Johnson."
A major challenge Morrison will face is boosting growth in Campbell's core soup brands, which already dominate the U.S. market and are growing abroad, analysts said.

Morrison joined Campbell in 1995 after establishing a reputation as a marketing wizard at PepsiCo Inc's Frito-Lay unit. He showed dramatic growth in Campbell's Pepperidge Farm snacks unit before being named head of the international and specialty foods division.

"That's what the next several months are going to be about. How do we take the momentum garnered in the various divisions under Morrison, such as the bakery area, and transalate that to the other areas of the company?" Teitelbaum said. "There is no question in my opinion that this man is very well suited for the task," he said.

Robert Bernstock, the president of Campbell's U.S. grocery division, who was also regarded as a contender in what McMillin called a "dog-fight" to succeed Johnson, was given the new title of executive vice president in the succession plan.
"They clearly went with a growth-manager (in Morrison)," McMillin said. "He's turned (Pepperidge Farm) Goldfish into a monster."
"The key now is will they be able to hold on to Bernstock?" he said.
Pinheiro said he had spoken Monday with Bernstock and described him as still happy with his situation, where he is responsible for more than half of Campbell's profits.
"I'm sure he's going to be compensated handsomely to ensure that he does remain," Pinheiro said.

Another key move in the succession was the elevation to executive vice president of Chief Financial Officer Basil Anderson, a former Scott Paper Co executive and key engineer of that firm's turnaround under Al Dunlap, Teitelbaum said.
"This is going to be a very big team effort, Teitelbaum said. "We're going to need some very strong financial discipline to take this company up to the next notch."
